items.prompt: What actually happens when an object from space strikes the Moon's surface at high speed, forming a crater?

options.label: The object simply digs a hole the same size and shape as itself
options.feedback: At the speeds involved, the impact releases enormous energy all at once. The resulting crater is usually many times wider than whatever struck the surface, not a hole shaped like it.

options.label: The Moon's gravity pulls the object apart before it lands
options.feedback: The Moon's gravity is far too gentle to break an incoming object apart. What shatters it, if anything does, is the violence of the impact itself.

options.label: The impact happens so fast that the point of contact behaves like an explosion, blasting out rock and carving a bowl-shaped hollow far bigger than the object itself
options.feedback: That explosion-like release of energy is exactly what carves a crater so much wider than the object that caused it.

options.label: Heat from the Sun softens the ground where the object lands
options.feedback: Sunlight has nothing to do with how a crater forms. The same craters appear on the permanently shaded floors of polar craters, far from any warmth.

items.ok_line: The energy of the strike does the work, not the shape of whatever hit the ground.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to all that speed the instant the object meets solid rock.
items.exp_text: An object striking the Moon at the speeds typical of space debris carries enormous energy, and that energy has to go somewhere the instant it meets solid rock. Rather than simply pushing material aside the way a slow-moving object would, the impact releases its energy almost like a blast, shattering and throwing rock outward in every direction. What is left behind is a bowl far wider than the object that caused it, carved by the force of that release rather than by the object's own shape.

items.prompt: Why do craters on the Moon stay looking almost as sharp as the day they formed, sometimes for billions of years?

options.label: Because lunar rock is far harder than rock on Earth
options.feedback: Lunar rock isn't unusually hard. What keeps craters intact is the total absence of anything able to wear them down, not the strength of the material itself.

options.label: Because the Moon's low gravity stops craters from collapsing
options.feedback: Gravity does shape how a crater looks right after impact, but it isn't what keeps that shape unchanged for so long afterwards; the missing ingredient is anything capable of eroding it.

options.label: Because new craters are rare, so old ones are simply the only ones there
options.feedback: New craters do keep forming on the Moon over time. Old ones remain sharp not because nothing new arrives, but because nothing wears the old ones away.

options.label: With no wind, no flowing water and no weather of any kind, there is nothing on the Moon to wear a crater's shape down over time
options.feedback: That total absence of wind, water or weather is exactly why a lunar crater's shape has nothing working against it.

items.ok_title: Nothing here to wear it down
items.ok_line: No wind, no rain, no ice — nothing at all to soften a sharp edge.
items.ko_title: Not the rock, not gravity, not scarcity
items.ko_line: New craters do keep forming; ask instead what could possibly smooth an old one away, and come up empty.
items.exp_title: A shape with nothing working against it
items.exp_text: On Earth, wind, rain, rivers and growing plants steadily wear a crater's sharp edges down within a comparatively short stretch of time. The Moon has none of these: no atmosphere to carry wind or rain, no liquid water, nothing living to disturb the ground. With absolutely nothing acting against its shape, a lunar crater simply keeps looking the way it did on the day it formed, for as long as nothing else strikes it.

items.prompt: What are the large, dark, smooth patches visible on the Moon, sometimes called 'seas'?

options.label: Vast plains of solidified lava that once flooded huge, ancient impact basins and hardened into dark rock
options.feedback: That flooding of ancient basins by lava, later hardened into rock, is exactly what these dark plains are.

options.label: Actual bodies of water that dried up long ago
options.feedback: The Moon has never held liquid water on its surface. The smooth, dark plains are solid rock, formed from lava rather than any vanished sea.

options.label: Patches where the Moon's surface dust is a different colour
options.feedback: The dark colour goes far deeper than a dusting on top. These are separate plains of solidified lava, distinct in composition from the surrounding highlands, not merely a difference in surface dust.

options.label: Regions permanently covered in shadow
options.feedback: These plains are lit by the Sun just like the rest of the near side over the course of a lunar day. Their dark appearance comes from the rock itself, not from being shaded.

items.ok_line: The dark 'seas' are solid rock that once flowed as molten lava.
items.ko_title: Not water, not dust, not shadow
items.ko_line: These plains are lit by the Sun like anywhere else; the darkness comes from what the ground itself is made of.
items.exp_text: Long ago, some of the Moon's largest impact basins were flooded from below by molten rock that rose up through cracks in the crust. That lava spread out into wide, flat plains and then cooled and hardened into dark, iron-rich rock, quite different in colour from the paler rock surrounding it. What looks from Earth like the smooth, dark surface of a sea is really solid rock that was once a flood of lava.

items.prompt: What causes the bright streaks, or 'rays', that radiate outward from some of the Moon's craters?

options.label: Mineral deposits that seeped up from underground long after the crater formed
options.feedback: The rays appear at the same time as the crater itself, thrown out in the impact, rather than seeping up afterwards from below.

options.label: Material blasted out during the impact that formed the crater, scattered outward and left lying on top of the older, more sun-darkened surface around it
options.feedback: That freshly scattered material, sitting on top of older, darker ground, is exactly what produces the bright streaks.

options.label: Reflections of sunlight bouncing off nearby mountains
options.feedback: The streaks are a real physical layer of material spread across the ground, not an optical reflection from some other feature nearby.

options.label: Frost that has settled only in those particular patterns
options.feedback: The Moon has essentially no water to form frost across such wide areas. The streaks are freshly exposed rock and dust, not any kind of ice.

items.ok_line: Material blasted out during the impact, lying on top of older, duller ground.
items.ko_title: Not underground, not a reflection, not frost
items.ko_line: Whatever made these streaks arrived at the same instant as the crater itself.
items.exp_text: When an impact forms a crater, it doesn't just carve out a bowl, it also flings loose rock and dust outward across the surrounding surface, sometimes for a very long distance. That freshly exposed material reflects more sunlight than the older ground around it, which has spent ages being darkened by exposure to space. The bright streaks radiating outward are simply that scattered material, still sitting where the blast threw it.

items.prompt: What is the fine, powdery layer of 'moon dust', known as regolith, that covers the lunar surface?

options.label: Volcanic ash that settled after ancient eruptions
options.feedback: While some lunar rock did come from ancient volcanic activity, the fine, crushed layer covering the surface everywhere comes from constant small impacts, not ash fallout.

options.label: Sand blown into place by lunar wind
options.feedback: The Moon has no atmosphere and so no wind at all. Nothing has ever blown this material into place.

options.label: Solid rock ground down into fine powder and fragments over billions of years by countless small impacts
options.feedback: That relentless grinding by countless small impacts is exactly what has crushed the surface rock into this fine powder.

options.label: A layer of ice crystals mixed with rock
options.feedback: Most of the lunar surface is bone dry rock and dust. Only a few permanently shadowed spots near the poles hold any ice at all, and this widespread powder is not one of them.

items.ok_line: Countless small impacts, over an enormous stretch of time, crushing rock into powder.
items.ko_title: Not ash, not wind, not ice
items.ko_line: The Moon has no wind to blow anything and almost no ice; something else has been quietly working the surface instead.
items.exp_text: The Moon has no atmosphere to burn up incoming debris before it reaches the ground, so a constant rain of tiny impacts, most too small to leave a visible crater, strikes the surface without pause. Over billions of years, that relentless small-scale bombardment has cracked, shattered and re-shattered the surface rock into ever finer fragments. The fine, powdery layer covering nearly the whole Moon is simply the accumulated result of that grinding.

items.prompt: Why do the Moon's highland regions look noticeably paler than the dark maria nearby?

options.label: The highlands are covered in a fresh layer of frost
options.feedback: The Moon has essentially no ice outside a few permanently shadowed polar craters. The pale colour of the highlands comes from the rock itself, not frost.

options.label: The highlands are simply dustier than the maria
options.feedback: Fine dust covers both regions about equally. The colour difference comes from what kind of rock lies underneath that dust, not from how much dust sits on top.

options.label: The highlands catch more direct sunlight than the maria
options.feedback: Sunlight falls on the whole visible surface in much the same way over a lunar day. Brightness here comes from what the rock reflects, not from any region catching extra light.

options.label: The highlands are made of a different kind of rock that reflects more sunlight than the darker, iron-rich rock that makes up the maria
options.feedback: That difference in rock type, one paler and more reflective, the other dark and iron-rich, is exactly what sets the two regions apart in colour.

items.ok_line: The highlands are built from a paler kind of rock than the dark maria nearby.
items.ko_title: Not frost, not dust, not extra light
items.ko_line: Both regions get roughly the same sunlight and the same coating of dust; look instead at what lies underneath.
items.exp_title: Two kinds of rock, two shades
items.exp_text: The Moon's highlands are made largely of a pale rock that formed early in the Moon's history, rich in light-coloured minerals that reflect sunlight fairly well. The maria nearby are built from a much darker, iron-rich rock that solidified later from flowing lava, and that rock absorbs far more of the sunlight falling on it than it reflects. The contrast in colour visible from Earth traces straight back to this difference in the rock itself, not to how much light either region happens to receive.

items.prompt: Why do temperatures on the Moon's surface swing to such extremes between lunar day and lunar night?

options.label: With no atmosphere to trap heat or spread it around, the surface loses whatever warmth it gains almost as soon as the Sun goes down
options.feedback: That missing blanket of atmosphere, unable to trap or spread the heat, is exactly why the surface swings so far between hot and cold.

options.label: Because the Moon is much farther from the Sun than Earth is
options.feedback: The Moon orbits the Sun at essentially the same distance Earth does. The extreme swings come from what happens at the surface itself, not from being especially close to or far from the Sun.

options.label: Because lunar rock cools down faster than rock on Earth
options.feedback: The rock itself isn't unusual. What differs is that Earth's atmosphere holds and moves heat around long after sunset, and the Moon has no such blanket at all.

options.label: Because the Moon's poles are much colder than its equator, throwing off the average
options.feedback: The extremes described here happen at a single spot between its own day and its own night, not from comparing different regions of the Moon.

items.ok_title: No blanket to hold the heat
items.ok_line: Warmth builds up fast in sunlight and escapes just as fast once the Sun is gone.
items.ko_title: Not distance, not the rock, not the poles
items.ko_line: The Moon sits about as far from the Sun as Earth does; think instead about what Earth has that the Moon simply doesn't.
items.exp_text: On Earth, the atmosphere absorbs and circulates heat, keeping the ground from swinging wildly between baking and freezing over the course of a day. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere to do any of that, so its surface heats up directly under sunlight and then radiates that heat straight back out into space the moment the Sun sets. Without any blanket of air to hold or spread the warmth around, a single spot on the Moon runs through an enormous temperature swing between its long day and its long night.

items.prompt: What causes 'moonquakes', the trembling occasionally detected within the Moon?

options.label: Ancient volcanoes that are still active today
options.feedback: The Moon's volcanic activity ended a very long time ago. The trembling detected today comes from flexing and slow internal changes, not from ongoing eruptions.

options.label: Earth's gravity flexing the Moon's solid body very slightly as their distance and alignment change, along with slow cooling and cracking deep inside
options.feedback: That slight flexing from Earth's gravity, together with the Moon's slow internal cooling, is exactly what releases the strain felt as a moonquake.

options.label: Loose rock sliding down the sides of craters
options.feedback: Surface rockslides do happen occasionally, but the deeper trembling that gives moonquakes their name comes from forces acting far below the surface, not from material shifting on top of it.

options.label: Sudden temperature changes cracking the surface rock
options.feedback: Temperature swings can crack rock near the surface, but the moonquakes felt deep within the Moon come from a different cause, tied to gravity acting on the whole body rather than heat and cold at the surface.

items.ok_line: Earth's gravity still tugs at the Moon's solid body, and that tug leaves a trace.
items.ko_title: Not volcanoes, not surface slides, not just heat and cold
items.ko_line: The trembling detected deep within the Moon comes from forces acting on the whole body, not from anything happening on the surface alone.
items.exp_title: A body still settling and flexing
items.exp_text: Even though the Moon is tidally locked, its distance from Earth and its exact orientation shift very slightly over each orbit, and Earth's gravity keeps flexing the Moon's solid body by a tiny amount as a result. Deep inside, the Moon is also still slowly cooling from its molten past, and that cooling lets old cracks shift and settle further. Both of these slow, ongoing processes release their built-up strain as the faint trembling known as a moonquake.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon have no wind, rain, or clouds of any kind?

options.label: Because the Moon is too cold for any weather to form
options.feedback: Cold alone doesn't rule out weather — plenty of very cold places on Earth still have wind, snow and cloud. What the Moon lacks is any atmosphere to make weather possible in the first place.

options.label: Because the Moon rotates too slowly to generate wind
options.feedback: Even a very slowly rotating world could have gentle winds if it had an atmosphere. The missing ingredient here is air itself, not rotation speed.

options.label: It has essentially no atmosphere, and without air to move as wind or hold moisture, none of the ingredients needed for weather exist there
options.feedback: That missing atmosphere is exactly the missing ingredient — no air means nothing to move as wind and nothing to carry moisture.

options.label: Because sunlight cannot reach the Moon's surface properly
options.feedback: Sunlight reaches the Moon's surface directly and strongly. The absence of weather has nothing to do with how much light arrives, only with the absence of any air to carry it as wind or cloud.

items.ok_line: Wind needs air to move, rain needs air to hold moisture — the Moon has neither.
items.ko_title: Not cold, not rotation, not sunlight
items.ko_line: Plenty of very cold, slowly turning places still have weather, as long as they have an atmosphere. Ask what the Moon is missing instead.
items.exp_text: Wind is simply air moving from one place to another, and clouds and rain depend on that same air being able to carry and release moisture. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere at all, so there is no air present to move as wind, hold any moisture, or gather into a cloud. Without that basic ingredient, none of the familiar weather Earth has can ever get started on the Moon.

items.prompt: Why do most craters on the Moon end up roughly circular, even when the object that made them struck the ground at a shallow, glancing angle?

options.label: Because almost every object happens to strike the Moon at a perfectly straight-down angle
options.feedback: Impactors arrive from every possible angle. A straight-down angle is not required, since even a glancing strike still tends to leave a round crater.

options.label: Because the Moon's gravity reshapes every crater into a circle after it forms
options.feedback: Gravity influences how a crater's walls settle, but it does not reach out afterwards and reshape an already-formed crater into a different outline.

options.label: Because only round objects ever survive long enough to hit the Moon
options.feedback: Incoming objects come in every shape. The roundness of the resulting crater comes from how the impact's energy is released, not from the shape of whatever caused it.

options.label: At the speeds involved, the impact releases its energy almost like an explosion spreading outward evenly in every direction, which produces a round crater regardless of the angle the object arrived at
options.feedback: That evenly spreading release of energy, however the object arrived, is exactly what leaves behind a round crater almost every time.

items.ok_title: An explosion doesn't remember the angle
items.ok_line: However the object arrived, the burst of energy spreads outward evenly and leaves a round scar.
items.ko_title: Not straight-down only, not reshaped later, not a matter of shape
items.ko_line: Impactors strike from every angle, and nothing comes along afterwards to round off an already-formed crater.
items.exp_title: Round from the blast, not the approach
items.exp_text: An incoming object can strike the Moon from almost any direction, including at a low, glancing angle, yet the energy released at the moment of impact still turns into something close to an even burst outward in all directions. That even release of energy is what actually carves the crater, largely overwhelming any hint of the original direction the object was travelling. As a result, the great majority of craters come out looking round, whatever angle produced them.
